chapter.name: The World of Numbers
chapter.blurb: Natural numbers, zero and integers, rational numbers and their arithmetic, irrational numbers, real numbers and decimal expansions.

scope_in.item: Natural numbers, zero as a number and integers with Brahmagupta's rules for zero and signed numbers
Rational numbers as p/q, equivalent forms, equality and the four operations, closure and the distributive law
Represent rational numbers on the number line, absolute value, distance |a - b| and density of rational numbers
Irrational numbers: root 2 is irrational by contradiction, construct root n on the number line, pi as irrational
Real numbers: decide if p/q has a terminating or repeating decimal from the prime factors of q; irrationals neither terminate nor repeat
Convert terminating, pure repeating and general repeating decimals into p/q; the cyclic number 142857; 0.999... = 1
End-of-chapter exercises on decimals, density, square root spiral and proof problems

scope_out.item: Laws of exponents and rationalising denominators
Complex or imaginary numbers beyond the mention of i
scope_out.reason: Only mentioned as a preview for later years

scope_out.item: Proofs that other roots or pi are irrational in full detail
scope_out.reason: Only root 2 is proved; others are left as Think and Reflect
Madhava's series for pi is only introduced; the study is left to higher grades

concepts.name: Natural numbers, zero and integers: Brahmagupta's rules
concepts.description: How counting gave natural numbers, how zero became a number and how negative numbers (debts) gave the integers, with Brahmagupta's rules for zero and signed numbers.
concepts.idea: Natural numbers count objects; zero and negative numbers extend them to the integers, where a fortune is positive and a debt is negative.
concepts.rule: a + 0 = a, a - 0 = a, a x 0 = 0, a - a = 0. Fortune + fortune = fortune; debt + debt = debt; debt x fortune = debt; debt x debt = fortune.
concepts.example: (-3) x (-4) = 12: removing four debts of 3 rupees each makes you 12 rupees richer.

concepts.name: Rational numbers and their arithmetic
concepts.description: The definition p/q with q not zero, equivalent forms, equality, the four operations, commutative and distributive laws and closure.
concepts.idea: A rational number is a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator, and it has many equivalent forms.
concepts.rule: a/b = c/d if ad = bc. a/b + c/b = (a + c)/b. (a/b) x (c/d) = ac/bd. (a/b) / (c/d) = ad/bc. Rational numbers are closed under +, -, x and division by a non-zero number.
concepts.example: 12/30 = 2/5 after dividing top and bottom by 6; -1/3 = -2/6 = -3/9.

concepts.name: Rational numbers on the number line, absolute value and density
concepts.description: Locating p/q on the number line, absolute value and distance, and the fact that there are infinitely many rationals between two rationals.
concepts.idea: To place p/q, divide each unit interval into q equal parts and move p parts; between any two rationals lies another, their average.
concepts.rule: |x| is the distance of x from 0 and |x| >= 0. The distance between a and b is |a - b|. The average (a + b)/2 lies between a and b.
concepts.example: 9/4 = 2 and 1/4 lies between 2 and 3; the average of 1 and 3/2 is 5/4.

concepts.name: Irrational numbers and the proof that root 2 is irrational
concepts.description: Numbers that cannot be written as p/q, the proof by contradiction for root 2, constructing root n on the number line and pi.
concepts.idea: Some lengths, like the diagonal of a unit square, cannot be written as a ratio of integers.
concepts.rule: A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q with integers p and q (q not 0). Root 2 is irrational by contradiction: assuming root 2 = p/q in lowest terms forces p and q both to be even.
concepts.example: The diagonal d of a unit square has d^2 = 1 + 1 = 2, so d = root 2, which is irrational.

questions.q: How does the proof that root 2 is irrational end in a contradiction?
questions.a: It shows that p and q are both even, so they share the factor 2. That contradicts the assumption that p/q was in lowest terms (co-prime).
s: p and q are both even

questions.q: Prove by contradiction that root 3 is irrational.
questions.a: Assume root 3 = p/q in lowest terms. Then 3q^2 = p^2, so p^2 is a multiple of 3 and so is p; write p = 3k. Then 3q^2 = 9k^2 so q^2 = 3k^2 and q is also a multiple of 3. Then p and q share the factor 3, contradicting lowest terms.
s: Assumes root 3 = p/q in lowest terms and gets 3q^2 = p^2
Deduces p and then q are multiples of 3

concepts.name: Real numbers and decimal expansions: terminating or repeating
concepts.description: Real numbers as rational plus irrational numbers; deciding whether p/q has a terminating or repeating decimal from the prime factors of q.
concepts.idea: Dividing p by q either ends with remainder 0 or a remainder repeats, so the decimal terminates or repeats.
concepts.rule: In lowest terms, p/q terminates exactly when the prime factors of q are only 2, only 5 or both; the number of decimal places is the larger of the powers of 2 and 5 in q. Irrational numbers neither terminate nor repeat.
concepts.example: 3/20: 20 = 2^2 x 5, so 3/20 = 15/100 = 0.15 terminates; 1/7 repeats because its denominator has the prime factor 7.

questions.q: A rational number has a terminating decimal whose last non-zero digit is in the 4th decimal place. Show it can be written as p/10^4 with p not divisible by 10, and say if its lowest-form denominator must be divisible by 2^4 or 5^4.
questions.a: Multiplying by 10^4 gives an integer p, so the number is p/10^4. If 10 divided p the last non-zero digit would be earlier, so p is not divisible by 10, that is, not by both 2 and 5. So after cancelling, 2^4 or 5^4 (or both) stays in the denominator. Yes, it is necessary.
s: p is not divisible by 10 because otherwise the last non-zero digit would be earlier

concepts.name: Converting decimals to p/q and the cyclic patterns
concepts.description: Writing terminating, pure repeating and general repeating decimals as fractions; cyclic numbers such as 142857 and 0.999... = 1.
concepts.idea: Multiplying a repeating decimal by a power of 10 and subtracting removes the repeating tail.
concepts.rule: Pure repeating: x = decimal, multiply by 10^n (n repeating digits) and subtract. General: first multiply by 10^m (m non-repeating digits) then by 10^n and subtract.
